newsitem.title: INDIA: INDIA METALS - Zinc, lead recycle units face closure.
newsitem.headline: INDIA METALS - Zinc, lead recycle units face closure.

text.p: A ban on the import of zinc ash and lead scrap by India last year has pushed domestic recycling units to the brink of closure, industry leaders said on Wednesday.
"Secondary zinc and lead industries are in the doldrums," said V.R. Subramanian, a former executive director of India Lead, Zinc Information Centre and currently its consultant.

He said most secondary zinc and lead producers had either closed their factories or were on the verge of closure after India banned imports of zinc ash and lead scrap in April 1996 on the ground that they were hazardous.

There are about 35 secondary zinc manufacturers and 100 units employing about 50,000 people that make zinc sulphate, a micro-nutrient that is mixed with other fertilisers for use in zinc-deficient land.
A few secondary lead units and a number of backyard lead smelters have downed shutters in the past few months. These contributed about 20,000 tonnes of lead annually.
Subramanian said the absence of production from both secondary zinc and lead units had pushed up India's imports of these metals.
India's zinc consumption is estimated at 250,000 tonnes against a local availablility of about 150,000 tonnes. Before the ban, secondary zinc units supplied up to 35,000 tonnes.
"The deficit of about 100,000 tonnes needs to be plugged through imports," Subramanian said.
He said demand for zinc had been growing because of rising consumption by the galvanising and power generation industries.
Consumption of lead is estimated at 120,000 tonnes against a domestic production of 70,000 tonnes, and the gap bewteen demand and supply is about 50,000 tonnes.
"The worst sufferers are secondary zinc producers," said All-India Secondary Zinc Manufacturers' Association president Keshubhai Shah. "Most of the secondary zinc units are closed."

India banned import of zinc ash and skimmings and lead scrap following the Basel Convention in 1995 which banned the export of hazardous waste. Before that zinc ash, skimmings, dross and residues were allowed to be imported against a licence.
A working group of the Basel Convention, which subsequently met in February 1997 in Geneva placed zinc ash and skimmings on the list of non-hazardous meterials, Shah said.
He said India must not lose time in classifying zinc ash and skimmings as non-hazardous and instruct the Directorate of Foreign Trade to issue a notification to facilitate their imports.

Shah said countries of the European Union and OECD (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development) which banned trans-boundary movement of recyclable non-ferrous materials, had vested interests.
"These countries want to get cheap raw materials for their own recycling industries and export virgin metals to buyers such as India," Shah said.
"For instance, the zinc deficit is likely to increase at the rate of 3.0-6.0 percent per year. The gap will have to be bridged with imports which will grow continuously," he said.
India's Supreme Court has upheld the Basel Convention's ban on the movement of hazardous materials and another hearing of an appeal against the ban is scheduled next Monday.
"There's no ban on import of copper, nickel or tin scrap," noted Bombay Metal Exchange president Sharad Parikh. These are not considered hazardous.
